A quoted spread is not guaranteed profit, and obligations vary by market. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Publisher and editorial transparency Published by TradeHQ. Site creator: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date; the About page explains the site's editorial approach. In depth A market maker quotes prices at which it is prepared to buy and sell under applicable venue rules. The ask-minus-bid difference is a quoted spread, not a guaranteed realized profit. Quotes can change; fills, inventory price changes, hedging and operating costs affect results. Obligations and permitted conduct differ between markets. A decentralized automated market maker is a different mechanism that applies a pool pricing rule rather than the same dealer quoting arrangement. Do not infer that a displayed quote will fill an arbitrary quantity or that a market maker always earns money. TradeHQ does not reproduce order queues or dealer inventory. Key points Quote bid and ask prices under venue rules; liquidity is not guaranteed for every order A quoted spread is not guaranteed net profit Automated market makers use protocol pricing rules and liquidity pools rather than conventional dealer quotes Why it matters when you are learning Compare quoted bid and ask prices with actual executions. Spread changes can have multiple explanations and do not establish a participant’s intent or sophistication. Worked exercise and its limits Hypothetical quotes: buy at $10 and sell at $10.02. Buying 100 units then selling them all at that ask earns $2 gross only if both executions occur. Inventory loss, hedging and costs can exceed that spread; a quote is not guaranteed profit. A selected 10% NVDA fall contributes $280 of loss through the two exposures if other holdings stay unchanged and weights are fixed. Real fund weights need a dated holdings source; the assumed 10% is not a current portfolio fact. Timing and liquidity Distinguish a dated financial statement, guidance and an intraday price quote. old: The Greeks — Delta, Gamma, Theta & Vega Learning notes: The Greeks — Delta, Gamma, Theta & Vega These four Greeks describe model-based sensitivities to underlying prices, time and implied volatility; they do not guarantee realized price changes. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Derivatives contracts remain conceptual exercises. Educational only, not financial advice. Published by TradeHQ, created by Anuga Weerasinghe. Publisher background and editorial approach . No independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. Summary These four Greeks describe model-based sensitivities to underlying prices, time and implied volatility; they do not guarantee realized price changes. Why Greeks matter Greeks are model-based sensitivities to inputs, holding other inputs fixed. Delta describes underlying-price sensitivity; gamma describes a change in delta; theta describes time sensitivity; vega describes implied-volatility sensitivity. Interest rates and dividends can also matter. Finite market moves need not equal a first-order estimate, and different pricing models can produce different values. Delta — directional exposure A delta of 0.50 per share describes an approximate $0.50 option-price change for a $1 underlying move, with other inputs held fixed. For a 100-share contract that is about $50, before gamma and other effects. Some traders use delta as a rough probability shorthand, but it is not a calibrated real-world probability and need not match the model probability of finishing in the money. Gamma — how fast delta changes Gamma measures how delta changes as the underlying moves. It is often relatively large near the strike close to expiry, depending on volatility and other inputs. Dealer hedging can affect demand, but a chart or open-interest figure alone does not establish dealer positions, required hedges or the cause of a price move. Theta — the ticking clock Theta estimates an option value change as time passes under a model, holding other inputs fixed. State whether the quote is per share or per contract and whether a calendar or trading-day convention is used. Purchased options commonly have negative theta, but realised profit also depends on price, volatility and costs. Selling premium is not a guaranteed collection of that estimate. Vega — volatility sensitivity Vega estimates sensitivity to a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility, with other inputs held fixed. Implied volatility can change around earnings, but it need not rise before every release or fall afterwards. A long option can lose despite a favorable underlying move if time decay and a volatility decline offset that move. > Options have several model sensitivities: delta describes underlying-price sensitivity, gamma describes how delta changes with the underlying price, and theta and vega describe time and volatility sensitivities. Hold other model inputs fixed when interpreting each measure. (Educational only — not financial advice. TradeHQ offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. Options contracts, Greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) Key takeaways Delta estimates underlying-price sensitivity, not a guaranteed payoff or real-world event probability. Gamma is often relatively large near the strike close to expiration; volatility and other model inputs also matter. Theta is a model sensitivity; other price changes can offset or exceed it. Vega measures volatility sensitivity; a change in implied volatility is a different quantity. Check your understanding What does theta measure? Options: Directional exposure; Time decay per day; Volatility sensitivity; Interest-rate risk. Correct answer: Time decay per day. Why: Theta is a model estimate of time sensitivity with other inputs held fixed; units and time conventions must be stated. In the lesson example, a 0.50 delta and a $1 underlying rise imply approximately what change per option share, before other effects? Options: $0.10; $0.30; $0.50; $0.90. Correct answer: $0.50. Why: 0.50 × $1 = $0.50 per share, holding other inputs fixed; this is not an event probability. Which event can be followed by a sharp decline in implied volatility? Options: A fixed time every morning; An earnings announcement resolving uncertainty; Every market opening without exception; Every dividend payment without exception. Correct answer: An earnings announcement resolving uncertainty. Why: A sharp post-announcement decline in implied volatility is sometimes called IV crush. It is not confined to earnings and is not inevitable after an announcement. Which Greek measures the rate of change of delta? Options: Vega; Theta; Gamma; Rho. Correct answer: Gamma. Why: Gamma tells you how quickly delta itself changes.
